thread.title: Canadian bishops urge renewed concern over euthanasia law on 10th anniversary
thread.title_full: Canadian bishops urge renewed concern over euthanasia law on 10th anniversary

author: lax leader
title: Canadian bishops urge renewed concern over euthanasia law on 10th anniversary
text:
The Catholic bishops of Canada called on June 16 for Catholics and all people of goodwill to “voice renewed concern” about the country’s Medical Assistance in Dying law, which has now been in effect for a decade.
Parliament passed Bill C-14 in June 2016, legalizing medical assistance in dying (MAiD) for eligible adults under certain conditions. The law allows either direct administration of a lethal substance by a medical professional or self-administration with prescribed drugs. In their June 10 statement, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Standing Committee for Family and Life urged Canadians “to remain steadfast in opposing euthanasia and assisted suicide, to pray for the conversion of hearts and minds away from this practice, and to be present to persons who are sick and vulnerable.”
“We reject complacency with the status quo on euthanasia in Canada,” the bishops said. “Formed by the Gospel, we are called to draw near to those who suffer: not to ignore, trivialize, or abandon them in their pain or despair, but to accompany them with compassion, practical care, and hope (cf. Lk 10:30-37).” The statement also encouraged collaborative strategies that provide support for people living with serious illness or disability as well as their families.
Eligibility criteria currently require individuals requesting MAiD be at least 18 years old, mentally competent, eligible for publicly funded Canadian health services, have a serious incurable illness or disability causing intolerable suffering in an advanced state of irreversible decline. Requests must be voluntary without external pressure.
Individuals whose sole underlying condition is mental illness will become eligible for MAiD beginning March 17, 2027; however, an earlier expansion was delayed while Bill C-218 seeks to halt further broadening of eligibility. The bishops cited government data showing that MAiD accounted for 5.1% of all deaths nationwide—16,499 Canadians—in 2024 alone.
The bishops described Canada’s program as “the world’s largest and fastest-growing euthanasia program,” warning that expanded eligibility puts more Canadians at risk. They recalled that initially only those whose death was reasonably foreseeable were eligible, but legislation passed in 2021 broadened access further.
“True compassion does not answer suffering with death,” they said. Instead, they advocated presence alongside those who suffer through palliative care and relief from pain rather than hastening death. The bishops concluded by thanking communities resisting MAiD over the past decade: “Their witness reminds us that defending life is not only a public teaching but also a daily work of presence.” They ended their message with a prayer seeking comfort and strength for those suffering.
